The HR Vault has more new features that I'm really excited to share. 


Consultants have always had to work out which policies a client actually needs before they can build a handbook. Usually that's a few emails back and forth, or a call just to scope it out.
  
Now you get your own link to send straight to the client. They pick their business name, their tone, and tick the policies they want, all in plain English.
  
No login. No download. Just a short form and a thank you page, and an email notifying you that it's done!
  
Same handbook you'd have built anyway. Just a lot less chasing to get there and a lot less manual steps if you use the builder.

Every policy on the Vault (92 of them 😅) comes in three lengths too. Detailed for the very full picture, standard for... standard, and one-page (ish) for a quick reference summary.

content:
The ICO is changing its name from 30 September 🙄 


Current name: Information Commissioner

New name: Information Commission 

You may be wondering, as I did, why they are making such a small change to the name. 

“How many millions of my tax has this pointless exercise cost” was actually my thought 🫠 

The reason is that it will be moving away from one person (eg, the commissioner) being responsible to a board (eg, the commission) being responsible. 

I know! Just what we need, another committee making decisions - that’ll really speed their investigations up! 

Those of you who know your way around a data protection policy are probably now concluding that you’re going to spend the next year of your life removing an ‘er’ from every single document that mentions data. 

Good news. The DUAA says you can just leave as is, and there’s no need to ever change it if you don’t feel like it. 

The full legal update on The HR Vault can be read here: https://lnkd.in/g_hK9XzW 

Honestly. I wouldn’t waste your time on this one though. It’s the most pointless legal update ever written. 

If you want some actually helpful legal updates, subscribe to the Vault weekly newsletter on the page. 

And I’m just off to remove all instances of ‘er’ in Vault policies so you don’t have to!

content:
Louise Haigh today told the TUC conference that employers will have to "properly" consider flexible working requests before refusing them.


We already do 🫠

Consulting before refusal has been a legal requirement since April 2024 🫠

What she didn't dwell on is what's actually changing. Under the Employment Rights Act 2025, a tribunal won't just check whether you ran a fair process. It'll assess whether refusing was reasonable, full stop.

That's the change. 

From "did you follow the steps" to "was your business judgment good enough to survive a tribunal second-guessing it."

More time spent building a case for a decision you were already entitled to make. More exposure if a manager's reasoning doesn't hold up months later.

Small employers don't have an ER team for that. They have an owner-manager doing it between everything else. 

Nobody at the TUC conference is picking that up 🙄

This is meant to be "Make Work Pay." I'm struggling to see whose pay goes up.

Not the employee's. 

And not the small business owner's, who now spends more time and money defending decisions instead of running the place.

"The biggest uplift in workers' rights in a generation," Ms Haigh called the Act. It's certainly the biggest uplift in paperwork.

"Kids to pick up, parents to look after" is true and completely beside the point. The point is who's carrying the extra risk of getting the judgment call wrong - and it isn't the government.

I'd love to see the impact assessment on this one 😅

content:
Another new claim for employees to bring…


…another claim that doesn’t stand alone. 

Like the requirement for the statement of particulars, prevention of sexual harassment and a variety of others I can’t be bothered to recall, this one will not stand alone. 

In English, this means that it can’t be the only thing brought to the tribunal. Another claim, such as unfair dismissal, has to be successful first. 

This one is telling employees about their right to join a trade union. 

🙄🙄🙄 

I think it’s pretty obvious to anyone that knows me: I’m not a fan of what the government are doing to employers. 

I hate this sort of legislation, because it’s not actually benefiting anyone in my opinion. Everyone knows about trade unions. 

And it’s not actually really enforced, is it? 

Sure, the chances of a claim being brought against an employer are higher than ever. We have a smaller workforce and a flooded Tribunal system, therefore, more chance. 

But they are still small. 

And some lawyers have some aggressive tactics to force/frighten claimants into settling (🤮). 

Most claims drop off before they hit the courtroom. 

So employers don’t really have much motivation to bother with these things. 

And don’t really care. 

But, HR colleagues, I’m about you. We will be in trouble if we don’t advise about this! 

You can find an article about the guidance we have to date on The HR Vault here: https://lnkd.in/gxkAay4P

Spoiler alert: there’s about six weeks until this legislation goes live and there’s no final guidance yet. 

Oh wait, that’s not a spoiler! This is always what happens!
